opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think these systems are remarkable at producing images that look plausible, often stunning. But when you probe them, it becomes clear that they don't understand what they're depicting in the way we do. A simple example: ask for "a red cube on top of a blue sphere," or "a horse riding an astronaut," and the system often gets the relationships wrong. It gives you a red cube and a blue sphere, but in the wrong arrangement, or it reverts to the more typical astronaut riding a horse. That tells you it has learned strong statistical associations between words and visual features, but not compositional structure, the idea that the relations between objects matter and can be recombined in new ways.

Counting is another revealing case. Ask for exactly five apples and you might get four or seven. Text inside images is often gibberish. And hands, at least in earlier versions, had the wrong number of fingers. None of these are deep failures in isolation, but together they suggest the system has no underlying model of objects as things that persist, have parts, and obey physical constraints.

So I interpret these limitations as a window into what's missing: a conceptual understanding of the world. Humans have core knowledge, about objects, space, number, causality, that we build everything else on. These systems are trained to match the statistics of pixels to the statistics of captions, and that gets you surprisingly far, but it isn't the same as knowing what a cube is, or what "on top of" means.

I'd also caution against reading too much into the successes. When a system produces a beautiful image of exactly what you asked for, it's tempting to attribute understanding to it. That's the same anthropomorphism we fall into with language models. The real test is robustness: does it handle novel combinations, unusual phrasings, things that are rare in the training data? That's where the gaps show up, and I think that's where we should focus if we want to know what these systems really understand.

r001.rationale: The response says the systems do not understand what they depict and cites relational and compositional failures as evidence.

r002.rationale: It describes missing conceptual understanding and physical constraints, but does not say that lacking experience interacting with the physical world prevents human-level semantic ability.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that these systems are extraordinarily impressive at what they do, and that very impressiveness is what makes the question tricky. When DALL-E or Stable Diffusion produces a beautiful, coherent image of, say, an astronaut riding a horse, it's very tempting to say the system "understands" astronauts and horses and riding. But I'd push back on that framing.

What these systems have learned is a very sophisticated set of statistical correlations between words and visual features. They're remarkably good at the texture and style and surface composition of images. Where they fall down is exactly where you'd expect a system without a model of the world to fall down: compositionality, spatial relations, counting, cause and effect. You ask for "a red cube on top of a blue sphere" and you may get the colors swapped, or the objects side by side. You ask for a person with five fingers and you get seven. You ask for a glass of wine that's been knocked over and you often get an upright glass with some wine splashed around it, because the system doesn't have a notion of what knocking over a glass actually does.

I think of this as the difference between knowing what things look like and knowing what things are. Humans understand that a horse has four legs not because we've seen a lot of pixels, but because we have a concept of a horse as a physical object with a body plan, that legs support weight, that there are constraints on how bodies can be arranged. These systems are, in a sense, doing something closer to very good pastiche. And the errors they make are revealing precisely because they're errors no human, even a child, would make.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that this gets at a deeper issue in how we evaluate AI systems generally. We tend to look at the successes, which can be dazzling, and generalize from them to assume there's a coherent understanding underneath. But understanding, in the sense I care about, means having abstractions you can apply robustly in new situations, that let you reason about things you haven't seen. The failure modes of text-to-image systems suggest that the abstractions aren't really there, or they're there in a very brittle form. So I'd say these systems understand images about as well as a language model understands text, which is to say, in a way that is sometimes useful but is quite different from what we mean when we say a person understands something.

r001.rationale: It treats failures in spatial relations, counting, and cause and effect as evidence that the systems lack robust abstractions and do not understand what the depicted things are.

r002.rationale: It contrasts human concepts of physical objects with the systems’ lack of a world model, but does not say that lacking experience interacting with the physical world prevents human-level semantic abilities.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to distinguish between being able to generate an image that looks as though you understand something and actually understanding it. These systems are remarkably good at capturing visual patterns and associations between words and images. But that doesn’t necessarily mean they understand the objects in an image, how those objects relate to one another, or how they behave in the world.

For example, a system might generate very convincing individual objects but struggle when you specify a particular spatial relationship or a particular number of them. And that’s interesting because the image can look beautiful and realistic while still missing something essential in the request.

I wouldn’t say that this proves they have no understanding at all. I think understanding has different dimensions. But producing a convincing picture isn’t, by itself, a sufficient test. We need to ask how robustly the system can use the concepts we’re attributing to it, especially in unfamiliar combinations.

r001.rationale: The response links failures with object relationships and quantities to systems missing something essential, and says a convincing image alone does not show that they understand the concepts involved.

r002.rationale: The response mentions objects’ behavior in the world but does not say that lacking physical-world interaction prevents human-level semantic abilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be careful about what we infer from the images themselves. A system can produce a picture that looks remarkably sophisticated to us, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it understands the objects or the relationships in that picture. We supply a lot of the interpretation when we look at it.

One way to probe that is to ask for something that involves familiar concepts in an unfamiliar combination, especially spatial relationships or a particular number of objects. These systems can produce very convincing textures and styles while still failing to satisfy those constraints. That suggests there’s a gap between learning statistical associations and having concepts you can use reliably across different situations.

I wouldn’t say that means they understand nothing. I think the interesting question is what kind of understanding they have, and how robust it is. A beautiful image alone doesn’t answer that question.

r001.rationale: The response says failures on spatial and object-count constraints reveal a gap between statistical associations and reliably usable concepts, and cautions that convincing images do not show understanding of their objects or relationships.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention physical-world interaction or say that its absence prevents human-level semantic abilities.
